title: Secrets Management
summary: Where secrets should live instead of source code or config files, and how rotation limits the damage when one leaks anyway.

slides.markdown:
A **secret** is any credential a system needs to function that would cause damage if it leaked — a database password, an API key, a signing key, a certificate's private key. Every real application has dozens of them, and where they live is one of the highest-leverage security decisions a team makes, because a leaked secret is almost always a direct path to a breach, not just a contributing factor.

The pattern this topic builds toward: secrets belong in a **dedicated, access-controlled system** — never in source code, checked-in config, or container images — and even when that's done right, a leaked secret can still happen. **Rotation** is what limits the damage when it does.

slides.sectionTitle: Why secrets don't belong in source code
slides.subTitle: Or checked-in config, or container images
slides.markdown:
Three common places secrets end up that all share the same flaw: **git history is permanent**. A secret committed to source control and later "removed" in a follow-up commit is still sitting in every earlier commit, retrievable by anyone with read access to the repository's history — deleting the current file doesn't delete the history.

- **Source code** — hardcoded strings, found by anyone who can read the repo, forever, even after removal.
- **Checked-in config files** — same problem, one layer removed; `.env` files committed "just this once" are one of the most common real leak sources.
- **Container images** — a secret baked into an image layer during build persists in that layer even if a later layer deletes the file, and is extractable by anyone who can pull the image.

The common fix across all three: secrets should never be written to disk or committed anywhere in the build or source pipeline — they should be fetched from a dedicated system at the moment they're needed.

slides.subTitle: Centralized, access-controlled retrieval
slides.markdown:
A **secrets manager** (or vault) is a dedicated system built specifically to store secrets and hand them out under access control — think HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, GCP Secret Manager. Instead of a secret living in a config file, it lives in the vault, and application code authenticates to the vault (usually via its own workload identity, not another secret) and requests exactly the secret it needs at runtime.

This buys three things a plain config file can't: **centralized access control** (who and what can read which secret, enforced and auditable in one place), **audit logging** (every access to a secret is recorded — who read it, when, from where), and a **single place to rotate from** (update the secret in the vault once, and every consumer that fetches it at runtime picks up the new value, instead of hunting down every config file it was copy-pasted into).

The access-control piece is the one that matters most in practice: a config file grants "whoever can read this file gets the secret," while a vault can grant "only this specific service identity, only this specific secret, only from this specific environment."

slides.sectionTitle: Static long-lived secrets vs short-lived/dynamic secrets
slides.markdown:
| | Static long-lived secret | Short-lived / dynamic secret |
|---|---|---|
| Lifetime | Fixed, often unchanged for months or years | Minutes to hours, generated per request |
| Issued by | Manually created once, stored, reused everywhere | Generated on demand by the vault, unique per consumer |
| Exposure if leaked | Valid until someone notices and manually rotates it | Expires on its own shortly after issuance |
| Example | A database password set once and shared across every service | A vault dynamically creating a unique, time-limited database credential per request |

A **dynamic secret** is generated by the vault at the moment it's requested — a unique database user with a TTL, say — rather than handed out from a fixed pool. Two services never even share the same literal credential, and a leak from one consumer doesn't expose every other consumer's access. This is the secrets-management analogue of the role-assumption pattern in cloud IAM: minimize how long any single secret is valid, and how widely it's shared, rather than relying on a strong secret staying secret forever.

slides.sectionTitle: Injecting secrets at runtime instead of build time
slides.markdown:
**Build-time** injection bakes a secret into an artifact — a container image layer, a compiled binary, a build cache — at the moment it's built. That artifact then carries the secret everywhere it goes, including to registries, caches, and anyone who can pull or inspect it, for as long as that artifact exists, independent of whether the secret itself later rotates.

**Runtime** injection fetches the secret only when the running process actually needs it — an environment variable populated by the orchestrator from a vault at container start, or a sidecar that mounts a secret as an in-memory file, refreshed on rotation. The artifact itself never contains the secret; only the running instance, for as long as it runs, does.

The practical difference shows up the moment you rotate a secret: with runtime injection, restarting or refreshing the running workload picks up the new value automatically. With build-time injection, the secret is frozen into every image you've ever built with it — rotating it does nothing for images already sitting in a registry, which is a real, often-missed gap during incident response.

slides.sectionTitle: Rotation on a schedule vs rotation on suspected compromise
slides.markdown:
| | Scheduled rotation | Compromise-triggered rotation |
|---|---|---|
| Trigger | A fixed interval (e.g. every 90 days) | A specific signal — a leaked credential found in a log, a public repo, or an alert |
| Purpose | Limits how long *any* secret, leaked or not, stays valid — reduces the average exposure window | Responds to a known, specific exposure immediately |
| Urgency | Routine, planned, low-drama | Immediate, often paired with incident response |
| Failure mode if missing | A secret leaked between scheduled rotations stays valid for up to the full interval | A leaked secret stays valid indefinitely if no one ever finds out it leaked |

Both matter, and neither substitutes for the other. Scheduled rotation catches leaks you never find out about — the whole point is that it doesn't require detecting anything. Compromise-triggered rotation is faster than waiting for the next scheduled cycle when you *do* know something leaked, and treating a known leak as "we'll catch it on the next scheduled rotation" leaves a real, avoidable exposure window open.

slides.subTitle: The senior-level nuance
slides.markdown:
A subtlety that goes past "use a vault": the same logical secret often exists in multiple copies across environments — dev, staging, production — and each copy is a separate leak surface with, in practice, wildly different access controls. A staging database credential is frequently treated as lower-stakes and shared more loosely among a team, but if staging shares any network path or data with production (a common shortcut under deadline pressure), a leaked staging credential can become a production incident.

A mature secrets strategy treats every environment's secrets as independently sensitive, scoped to that environment's own vault namespace or instance, with access control that doesn't assume "it's just staging" is a meaningful risk reducer. It also means auditing not just "is this secret in a vault" but "how many copies of this logical secret exist, in how many environments, with how many different access policies" — sprawl is often the real problem, not any single storage location being wrong.

slides.sectionTitle: Rotating a leaked secret without revoking the old one
slides.markdown:
The pitfall, in either direction: rotating a leaked secret by generating a new one but leaving the old, leaked one still valid — or revoking the old one before the new one is fully propagated, causing an outage. Both come from treating rotation as a single atomic step instead of a two-part operation.

**Generate-then-fail-to-revoke** is the more dangerous half: a new secret is issued, systems are updated to use it, and everyone considers the incident closed — but the *old* leaked secret, unless explicitly revoked or invalidated, may still work. An attacker who has it is unaffected by your rotation.

**Revoke-before-propagate** is the availability-risk half: killing the old secret before every consumer has actually picked up the new one causes a self-inflicted outage across whatever hasn't updated yet.

The correct sequence, and worth stating explicitly in an incident response: issue the new secret, confirm every known consumer has switched to it (via monitoring, not assumption), *then* explicitly revoke the old one — and track down every consumer, including any you suspect might exist but haven't confirmed, because an unknown consumer still using the old secret after revocation is a different, but equally real, failure.

The practices above assume secrets are already living somewhere they shouldn't and need cleanup — but the cheapest fix is preventing the leak from happening at all. **Secret scanning** tools (git-secrets, TruffleHog, provider-native scanners like GitHub's push protection) run against commits, pull requests, and even build artifacts, matching against known secret formats (API key patterns, private key headers) and blocking or flagging a commit before it ever lands in history.

The highest-leverage place to run this is **pre-commit or pre-push**, catching a secret before it enters git history at all — because once it's in history, the leak has already happened even if the file is deleted in the very next commit. A CI-stage scan is a useful second layer, but it's already too late to prevent the secret from existing in the repository's permanent history; it can only catch it before deployment.

This is the one part of secrets management that's nearly free to adopt and catches the most common real-world mistake — an engineer pasting a working credential into code to test something quickly and forgetting to remove it before committing.
